column3: This is VLA Forge. A company describes its line in plain words, and gets a trained robot policy for each station in minutes. All of this runs in simulation.
Here's a new kitting line. Red parts go to the blue tote, yellow parts to the green one, and a ViperX at the end catches the rest.
The planner turns that into a chain of three stations: a VLA, then a VLA, then a scripted cell. Each VLA is fine-tuned from the closest skill in the library.
Now both stations train for real. The forge collects demos, fine-tunes, then tests each policy on scenes it never saw. The waiting is sped up four times, and the badge shows it.
The {rname} station got {r1} of {rn} on its first round, under the bar, so the critic sent it back for another.
The {a} station trained in {t0} seconds and the {b} one in {t1}. On {n} held-out scenes, they got {s0} and {s1}.
Then {parts} parts go down the belt, in simulation.
{done} of {parts} ended up in the right tote, at about {tpm} parts a minute in simulated time.
Each station's skill is saved in the library as a tile with its measured success.
Ask for something the arm can't reach, like lifting a block sixty centimeters, and the router says not feasible. The jaws top out at fifty-three.
In the Robot tab you build the arm itself. Every part has a preview, and each one is a real open-source model.
From typing that line to a finished run took under {mins} minutes.
